newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO talks resume on Hebron, ease tensions.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO talks resume on Hebron, ease tensions.

text.p: Israel and the PLO resumed talks on Monday on an Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron, signalling an easing of tensions over settlements and shootings.

Yitzhak Molcho, an adviser to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, met Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat in Jerusalem to end a 10-day break in the talks and try to clinch an elusive agreement, PLO officials said.

Israel and the PLO have failed in nearly three months of negotiations to agree on security arrangements which Netanyahu wants to protect some 400 Jews who live and study in the heart of Hebron amid more than 100,000 Palestinians.
A PLO official, who asked not to be identified, said a U.S.-arranged meeting on Sunday between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli officials had cleared the air for now.
"The meeting eased the tension that was building up between the two sides but we still have to wait and see how the attitude will be in the (Hebron) talks," the official said.

Israeli-PLO tensions flared in the last week over Israel's decision to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank, the killing of two settlers by Arab gunmen and the fatal shooting of an Arab worker by a Jewish farmer.
The White House, the main broker in Israeli-PLO talks, said on Monday it found the latest Israeli policy on settlements a complicating factor in efforts to reach peace in the region.
"It is troubling to see sides pre-empt issues that are under discussion by taking positions," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry told reporters.
Netanyahu sent Molcho and Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh to see Arafat in self-ruled Gaza late on Sunday and then spoke to the Palestinian leader by telephone.
"The important thing concerning the meeting is the continuity of the peace process and we are insisting to carry on this line," Arafat told reporters on Monday.
The PLO official told Reuters that Netanyahu and Arafat agreed that Molcho and Erekat would meet and would jointly brief the two leaders after each round of their talks.
The Palestinian official said Sunday's meeting in Gaza was arranged by U.S. ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk and U.S. Consul-General Edward Abington.

"I think the main issue was to ease the tension which existed between the two sides, especially after the terrorist clash on Wednesday," said David Bar-Illan, Netanyahu's communications chief, referring to the killing by Arab militants of a settler and her 12-year-old son.
Arafat earlier reacted angrily to Israel's decision to grant financial benefits, such as tax breaks, to West Bank settlers, describing the move as a timebomb.
About 130,000 Jews live in settlements scattered among two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, areas captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Three former U.S. secretaries of state and five other former American officials urged Israel in a letter to refrain from expanding Jewish settlements.

"We are concerned that unilateral actions, such as the expansion of settlements, would be strongly counterproductive to the goal of a negotiated solution," said the letter, addressed to Netanyahu and faxed to Reuters by his office.

The letter was signed by former secretaries of state James Baker, Lawrence Eagleburger and Cyrus Vance along with former senior government officials Zbigniew Brzezinski, Frank Carlucci, Brent Scowcroft, Richard Fairbanks and Robert Strauss.
